slides.text: The California Zephyr was stranded forty miles west of Denver, halted by an avalanche across the tracks during an unseasonable April blizzard. With the heating reduced to conserve fuel and phone reception dead, passengers huddled in the observation car beneath wool blankets. Sitting across the aisle from Claire was a quiet architect named Julian, who spent the first three hours methodically folding paper napkins and train receipts into intricate origami cranes, stags, and foxes without saying a word.

Whenever Claire looked away to watch the snowdrift against the glass, Julian would slide a newly folded creature onto the wooden armrest between them: a crane with its wings tilted toward her coffee cup; a miniature fox curled asleep beside her sketchbook. In return, Claire, an illustrator, used her charcoal pencil to draw tiny landscapes on paper napkins for his paper menagerie—a mountain ridge for the stag, a bamboo thicket for the crane. Neither of them broke the silence.

When the plows finally cleared the tracks at dawn and the train pulled into Union Station, the crowd surged toward the platform doors. Claire turned back, but Julian’s seat was already empty. Her heart sank—until she noticed one last origami creature left on the windowsill: a paper swallow with wings outstretched. Claire gently unfolded the tiny creases. Written across the inside of the receipt in pencil was: 'Some journeys take forty years. Thank you for giving me twenty-four hours of spring. Call me.'
